title: The Learning Log
subtitle: Learning in public, one month at a time.
meta_description: A monthly journal on building expertise in computer science, AI engineering, research and measurement science — including the months that did not go well.
lede: A monthly record of what I studied, what I built, and where I was wrong. It is kept in public because a claim nobody can check is not evidence of anything.
standard: This is a journal, not a transcript. Reading a paper is not finishing a course, and finishing a course is not competence. Where an entry claims I learned something, it should point at something I made, broke, or can explain without help.

entries.title: Learning to Think With AI, Not Just Build With It
entries.summary: No coursework finished this month. What I did instead was decide how I want to work with these tools before I accumulate any more of it — and write the rules down somewhere I can be held to them.

body.text: I am starting this log because I have a problem I cannot measure. My output has gone up. I am not at all sure my understanding has. Those two things can move independently, and for most of this year I have been tracking only the first one.

The thing that made it concrete was Sean Goedecke's essay **LLMs Reward Expertise**. His argument, as I read it, is that these models pay out in proportion to what you already know: an expert gets leverage from them, and a novice gets plausible output they cannot evaluate. I am not going to pretend I have tested that claim. It simply described something I recognised.
The gap between my work and my understanding is not visible from the outside. It is barely visible from the inside.

Miles Cranmer's talk on avoiding AI brain rot pushed on the same nerve from the research side — the worry that fluent assistance erodes the slow, uncomfortable work where understanding actually forms. Again: his framing, not my finding. I am recording where the ideas came from so that later I can tell which conclusions I earned and which I borrowed.
Six things I am currently turning over

items: AI can raise the quality and speed of my work without raising my understanding at all. These are separate variables and I have only been watching one.
Evaluating an AI output is a domain skill. Without it I cannot tell a sound answer from a confident one, which means I cannot safely use the tool at the exact moments it matters most.
I want to attempt hard problems myself before reaching for a solution — not out of purity, but because the struggle is where the mental model gets built.
A tool that agrees with me is less useful than one that argues. I should be asking these models to attack my reasoning, not to ratify it.
The real test is whether I can explain, test, debug and defend what I build when nothing is helping me.
Progress should be measured in evidence, not in the number of courses, tools or repositories I have started. I have started a lot of things.

body.text: I want to be careful about the status of these. They are not conclusions. They are hypotheses about my own working habits, and I have not yet run the experiment.
Five rules I am going to try
Principles that cannot be violated are not principles, they are decoration. Each of these can be broken, and I will know when I break it.

items.rule: Write my own problem statement, proposed architecture and success criteria first. If I cannot state what done looks like, I am not ready to ask anything for help.
Use the model to surface tradeoffs and attack my assumptions, not to make the decisions. The design should stay mine.
Read the critical path, reproduce the failures myself, review the tests, and explain the implementation with no assistance open.
Attempt the problem cold. Ask for a hint before an answer, and an answer only after the hint fails.
State the hypothesis and what would falsify it before asking anything to explore approaches. Otherwise I will find support for whatever I already believed.

body.text: The obvious failure mode is that this becomes a performance — a tidy list of virtuous habits that makes me feel rigorous without changing what I do on a Tuesday afternoon under deadline. The second failure mode is the opposite: refusing help on principle and being slower for no gain. I do not yet know where the line sits, and I suspect it moves depending on whether I am working inside my competence or outside it.

There is also a measurement problem I have not solved. *Can I explain this without help* is the test I keep reaching for, and it is a bad test, because I am the one grading it. I would like something harder to fake.
How I will know if this is working

Not by this entry. By whether the next several contain specifics — a bug I misdiagnosed and why, a result that contradicted what I expected, an explanation I could not give. If the months ahead read as smoothly as this one, that is the signal that I am writing a brochure rather than a log.

entries.next_focus: Start the first course properly and put the five rules under load: attempt the problem sets cold, and record honestly where I reached for help and whether it was warranted. One worked example of a misdiagnosis, written up, would be worth more than this whole entry.
